slides.title: Differentiation Theory
slides.notes: Open the lecture by treating differentiation as the operation that turns a small geometric view into linear data. In geometric measure theory the question is not only whether every point has a derivative, but which points are numerous enough to control area, tangency, and later rectifiability arguments.

slides.title: Five Moves From Limits To Tangents
slides.notes: Use this map as the promise for the room. The lecture begins with the classical blow-up definition, replaces ordinary limits by approximate limits, explains why Lipschitz control buys almost-everywhere differentiability, then ends with tangent cones and relative differentiation, which are the language needed for rectifiable sets.

slides.title: Ordinary Differentiability Is A Vanishing Error Ratio
slides.notes: Spend time on the quotient in the formula: the error is measured against the distance to the base point. A derivative is not just a best linear map, but a stable limit seen after rescaling the graph around a point while the nonlinear part disappears.

slides.title: Approximate Limits Ignore Null Dust, Not Bad Geometry
slides.notes: Approximate limits are the measure-theoretic compromise that makes differentiation useful on rough domains. The exceptional dust can be ignored only when it has density zero at the point. Stress that the word approximate is rigorous, not informal, because the density test decides which samples count.

slides.title: Coordinate Data Reassembles The Approximate Differential
slides.notes: The important theorem orientation is that coordinate information can be reassembled into a linear map at almost every point where the approximate partial derivatives exist. The slide should make students see why measurability and Fubini-style slicing enter before any tangent-plane picture becomes legitimate.

slides.title: Lipschitz Control Forces Differentiability Almost Everywhere
slides.notes: Rademacher's theorem is the first major payoff. A Lipschitz bound gives uniform control in every small ball, so one-dimensional differentiability along slices can be promoted to an approximate differential and then to an ordinary differential at almost every point. The proof strategy matters more here than the full technical proof.

slides.title: Finite Local Slope Organizes A Map Into Lipschitz Pieces
slides.notes: This slide separates local finite slope from global Lipschitz behavior. Stepanoff-type reasoning says that if the pointwise upper slope is finite on a set, the set can be organized into countably many pieces where the map behaves Lipschitzly. That decomposition is a recurring move in rectifiability.

slides.title: Higher Differentials Are Taylor Jets With Normed Remainders
slides.notes: Higher differentials should be presented as bookkeeping for Taylor jets, not as a new mystery. Each order records a symmetric multilinear piece, and the remainder condition says whether the jet genuinely approximates the function. This prepares Whitney extension without needing the audience to memorize the full compatibility formula.

slides.title: Whitney Extension Glues Compatible Local Predictions
slides.notes: Whitney extension is a repair theorem for data known only on a closed set. The compatibility tests prevent neighboring jets from contradicting each other, while a smooth partition of unity glues local polynomial predictions into one ambient function. Emphasize that the theorem creates ambient smoothness from local coherent data.

slides.title: Tangent Cones Record Directions That Survive Under Zoom
slides.notes: Tangent cones turn zooming into a definition that works for arbitrary subsets, not only smooth manifolds. The cone keeps every direction that can be approached by rescaled secants. For a smooth submanifold it collapses to the usual tangent space, which is why the definition is worth the abstraction.

slides.title: Relative Differentiation Restricts Ambient Linear Data
slides.notes: Relative differentiation answers the practical question of how to differentiate a function whose domain is itself a set. One extends locally to the ambient space, differentiates there, and then restricts the linear map to the tangent cone. On a submanifold this agrees with the coordinate-chart picture students already know.

slides.title: A Small Diagnostic For The Differentiation Habit
slides.notes: Connect the deck back to the notebook artifacts. The static visual is not a theorem proof; it is a finite diagnostic for the habit of the chapter. Students should name the local object, identify what the diagnostic treats as invariant, and predict exactly which hypothesis would fail under a bad perturbation.

slides.title: What Differentiation Theory Carries Forward
slides.notes: Close by previewing why this chapter is placed before rectifiability and currents. Differentiation supplies the local linear data, approximate limits tell us which points are typical, decompositions organize rough maps, and tangent cones give language for the geometry that survives under blow-up.
